21 - Meta analysis

Francisco E. Fonturbel

08/June/2026

A meta-analysis example based on the effectiveness of biological control on crop pests

Today we will use some data of Diaz-Siefer et al. 2022 as a working example. This dataset contains data of crop damage made by pest insects under different agricultural managment scenarios.

#Loading data file
data<-read.table("./data/21_data_meta_damage.txt", header = T)
attach(data)

#Loading packages required
library(meta)

Overall effects

How important is biological control on crop damage?

Let’s see it using a random-effects model:

overall.mod<-metacont(Ne, Xe, Se, Nc, Xc, Sc, data = data,
                      studlab = paste(caseID),
                      comb.fixed = FALSE,
                      comb.random = TRUE,
                      method.tau = "REML",
                      hakn = TRUE,
                      prediction = TRUE,
                      sm = "SMD",
                      method.smd = "Hedges")

summary(overall.mod)

Great! biological control has a significant overall effect on crop damage. Also, there is a significant heterogeneity in the model (which is expected in this kind of models)

Before examining the results using the moderator variables defined, we must assess the robustness of our data, using three tests:

(1) Funnel plot

funnel(overall.mod, studlab = TRUE)

Is there a significant bias on this? let’s test it;

metabias(overall.mod)
## Linear regression test of funnel plot asymmetry
## 
## Test result: t = 2.48, df = 55, p-value = 0.0162
## Bias estimate: 1.5849 (SE = 0.6390)
## 
## Details:
## - multiplicative residual heterogeneity variance (tau^2 = 2.3470)
## - predictor: standard error
## - weight:    inverse variance
## - reference: Egger et al. (1997), BMJ

Ooops! this funnel plot has a significant asymmetry problem. It seems that case D45 is making noise, let’s try again after excluding it.

data1<-data[-c(45),]
ovsens.mod<-metacont(Ne, Xe, Se, Nc, Xc, Sc, data = data1,
                      studlab = paste(caseID),
                      comb.fixed = FALSE,
                      comb.random = TRUE,
                      method.tau = "REML",
                      hakn = TRUE,
                      prediction = TRUE,
                      sm = "SMD",
                      method.smd = "Hedges")

## Linear regression test of funnel plot asymmetry
## 
## Test result: t = 2.25, df = 54, p-value = 0.0286
## Bias estimate: 1.5061 (SE = 0.6696)
## 
## Details:

## - predictor: standard error
## - weight:    inverse variance
## - reference: Egger et al. (1997), BMJ

Excluding D45 did not solve the problem.

(2) Baujat plot

The Baujat plot allows us to visually explore heterogeneity in our meta-analysis, visualizing the individual contribution of each case study on overall heterogeneity and the influence in the result.

baujat(overall.mod)

(3) Correlation

cor.test(overall.mod$TE, overall.mod$seTE, method="kendall", continuity = TRUE, alternative = "two.sided")
## 
##  Kendall's rank correlation tau
## 
## data:  overall.mod$TE and overall.mod$seTE
## z = 3.1046, p-value = 0.001905
## alternative hypothesis: true tau is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##      tau 
## 0.283208

We will examine the correlation between the effect size and sample size using Kendall’s approach.

Opps! we have a significant correlation in here.

(4) Trim & Fill

Duval & Twieedie’s approach ‘balances’ the model by trimming some case studies and filling others to balance the funnel plot (i.e., approaching to a symmetric model) and recalculates model estimates. If the meta-analysis is robust, we should not see any change in the direction and significance of the overall effect.

trimfill(overall.mod)
## Number of studies: k = 72 (with 15 added studies)
## Number of observations: o = 2259 (o.e = 1123, o.c = 1136)
## 
##                         SMD            95% CI    t p-value
## Random effects model 0.2262 [ 0.0409; 0.4114] 2.43  0.0174
## Prediction interval         [-1.0644; 1.5168]             
## 
## Quantifying heterogeneity (with 95% CIs):
##  tau^2 = 0.4106 [0.2653; 0.7143]; tau = 0.6408 [0.5150; 0.8452]
##  I^2 = 72.5% [65.3%; 78.3%]; H = 1.91 [1.70; 2.14]
## 
## Test of heterogeneity:
##       Q d.f.  p-value
##  258.59   71 < 0.0001
## 
## Details of meta-analysis methods:
## - Inverse variance method
## - Restricted maximum-likelihood estimator for tau^2
## - Q-Profile method for confidence interval of tau^2 and tau
## - Calculation of I^2 based on Q
## - Hartung-Knapp adjustment for random effects model (df = 71)
## - Prediction interval based on t-distribution (df = 71)
## - Trim-and-fill method to adjust for funnel plot asymmetry (L-estimator)

Well, well, well… it seems that our meta-analysis is robust and our results are reliable, despite the heterogeneity issues detected above. Now that we have checked it, we’ll examine our moderator variables to disentangle the complexity of these responses:

                      byvar = zone)
